title: A Sensor You Can Trust: Calibrate, Reject, Smooth, and Measure What It Cost

questions.question: A smoother is placed before a rejection filter. What happens to a single wild reading?
options: The smoother has already spread a share of it, alpha, into every later reading, where the rejection filter would have caught it whole: 0.200 of a spike of 50 against 0.000
questions.explanation: Reject while an outlier is still one reading.

questions.question: In what order should the stages run?
options: Calibrate, reject, smooth, so every stage works in real units and an outlier is rejected whole
questions.explanation: A raw 3.0 through a scale of 2 and an offset of 1 came out as 7.0000.

questions.question: A smoother at alpha 0.2 is fed noise of standard deviation 1. How much noise is left?
options: About 0.339, close to the square root of alpha over 2 minus alpha, which is 0.333

questions.question: How far behind a ramp does a smoother at alpha 0.2 run at 100 Hz?
options: 0.0400 s, which is (1 - alpha) / alpha samples
questions.explanation: The cost of smoothing, as a delay.

questions.question: What does a rejection filter do to a real step?
options: Holds it back by about half its window until enough of the window agrees: time to half way was 0.03 s at a window of 7 and 0.07 s at 15 with alpha 0.5, against 0.00 s with none
questions.explanation: A wide window rejects better and follows worse.

questions.question: Why build the table of four costs?
options: A quieter output lags more and no row is best, so the choice is made against the loop's own budget with the numbers in front of you rather than found out from a sluggish controller
